topicName: Token Permissions (GITHUB_TOKEN) and Least Privilege Principle
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Token Permissions (GITHUB_TOKEN) and Least Privilege Principle in GitHub Actions"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you run a workflow in GitHub Actions, GitHub automatically creates a unique GITHUB_TOKEN secret to authenticate your workflow runs. By default, this token has broad permissions depending on repository settings. Securing your workflows using the Principle of Least Privilege is critical to prevent supply chain attacks."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding the Default GITHUB_TOKEN Behavior"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, GitHub grants the GITHUB_TOKEN read and write access to most scopes if no explicit permissions are declared. This means any compromised dependency or malicious pull request running actions could potentially modify your repository, alter code, or leak sensitive data."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Applying the Least Privilege Principle"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Principle of Least Privilege dictates that a workflow should only have the exact permissions necessary to complete its task and nothing more. You can enforce this globally in your repository settings or explicitly per workflow file using the permissions key."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Permissions at the Workflow Level"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"To restrict permissions for an entire workflow, define the permissions block at the top level of your YAML file. This overrides the default repository settings, starting from a baseline of zero permissions."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"name: Secure Workflow
on: [push]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run build
        run: npm ci && npm run build"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Permissions at the Job Level"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"If a workflow contains multiple jobs that require different scopes, you can define the permissions block individually for each job."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"name: Multi-Job Workflow
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run lint

  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: node release-script.js"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Available Permission Scopes"},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"contents: Grants read or write access to repository contents, commits, branches, downloads, and code."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"issues: Grants read or write access to issues and their comments."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"pull-requests: Grants read or write access to pull requests, comments, and merging."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"packages: Grants read or write access to GitHub Packages."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"id-token: Required for fetching OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens for cloud provider authentication."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Token Security"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always start by setting top-level permissions to read-all or contents: read, then explicitly elevate permissions only where necessary."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid using write permissions on pull requests originating from forks, as malicious actors can exploit those tokens."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Regularly audit your organization and repository settings to enforce restrictive default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions."}]
